text:
QUEEN’S BENCH
FOR SASKATCHEWAN

Citation:
2020
SKQB 284

Date:
2020 10 30

Docket:                  DIV 82 of 2017

Judicial Centre:      Saskatoon

BETWEEN:

ANTHONY JOSEPH VAN BURGSTEDEN

PETITIONER

‑ and ‑

KIRSTEN
FAYE JEWITT

RESPONDENT

Counsel:

Patrick H. Loran
for the petitioner

Kirsten F. Jewitt
the respondent, appearing on her own behalf

Amanda D. Neudorf
for A.G. Canada (on the constitutional issue)

___________________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT                                                                                                         TURCOTTE
J.

October 30, 2020

___________________________________________________________________________

Introduction and Positions of the Parties

[
1
]

The parties were
married on August 10, 1991 and separated on March 29, 2015. On February 8,
2017, Mr. Van Burgsteden commenced divorce proceedings against Ms. Jewitt for a
civil divorce under
the
Divorce
Act
, RSC 1985, c 3 (2d Supp)
[
Divorce
Act
]. He alleges that
there has been a breakdown of the marriage and that it is no longer possible
for him to reconcile or resume cohabitation with Ms. Jewitt.

He also seeks an eq
ual division of the parties’ family home and family
property under
The
Family
Property Act
, SS 1997, c
F-6.3.

[
2
]

Ms. Jewitt filed an
answer and counterpetition on November 13, 2018. She opposes the divorce and
seeks spousal support under the
Divorce Act
and
spousal maintenance under
The

Family Maintenance Act, 1997
, SS 1997, c F-6.2. Further, she seeks an unequal division of their
family home and family property under
The
Family Property Act
.

[
3
]

Mr. Van Burgsteden
seeks to have the divorce proceeding severed from the parties’ corollary relief
and family property proceedings. Ms. Jewitt opposes his application on
constitutional and other grounds.

[
4
]

Ms. Jewitt challenges
the constitutionality of the
Divorce Act
. Broadly, she claims that
granting a divorce infringes her rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

in two ways:

1.   a civil
divorce discriminates against her on the basis of religion and does not uphold
the right to equal protection and benefit of the law as divorce is inconsistent
with her religious beliefs; and

2.   granting a
civil divorce violates her right to equal protection of the law on the basis of
mental disability because divorce, she argues, would exacerbate or contribute
to her mental disability.

[
5
]

Ms. Jewitt also claims
the
Divorce Act

is inconsistent with both the
Constitution Act, 1982
,
and the
Civil Marriage Act,
SC 2005, c 33 [
Civil Marriage Act
]
.

[
6
]

In addition to her own
evidence, Ms. Jewitt filed the affidavit of Pastor Virgil D. Anderson, a pastor
of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Canada, which denies the dissolution of
the covenant of marriage between the parties. Ms. Jewitt also has indicated
that she upholds the covenant of marriage and does not release the petitioner
from it.

[
7
]

Specifically, she
argues that granting a

divorce is contrary to the
Constitution Act,
1982
,

which acknowledges the supremacy of God in its preamble. She
claims that marriage ordained by God is a permanent institution severable only
by death. She argues the reference to the supremacy of God in the
Constitution
Act, 1982
,

incorporates this belief into the laws of Canada.
Additionally, in its preamble, the
Civil Marriage Act

recognizes
marriage as a fundamental institution of Canadian society to which the
Parliament of Canada has a responsibility to support. As a result, she claims
that granting a civil divorce under the
Divorce Act

is inconsistent with
the
Civil Marriage Act.

[
8
]

Finally, if her
constitutional arguments fail, Ms. Jewitt argues the Court cannot grant a severed
judgment for divorce without the consent of both parties. Further, she claims
the granting of a severed judgment for divorce will prejudice her other claims
in the proceeding. She is concerned that if the parties are no longer spouses
and Mr. Van Burgsteden dies before the other issues are resolved, she will not
be able to pursue her spousal support claim against his estate.

Issues

[
9
]

There are six issues to
be addressed in the constitutional questions raised by Ms. Jewitt:

(i)        Does granting a civil
divorce under the
Divorce
Act

discriminate against
Ms. Jewitt on the basis of religion, thereby infringing her rights under
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
?

(ii)       Does granting a civil divorce under the
Divorce Act

discriminate against Ms. Jewitt on the basis of mental
disability, thereby infringing her rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
?

(iii)     If Ms. Jewitt’s
s. 15(1)

Charter

rights are infringed, are the infringements saved by

s. 1
?

(iv)      If the infringements are
not saved under s. 1, what is the appropriate remedy?

(v)       Does the
Divorce Act

conflict with the preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1982
?

(vi)      Does the
Divorce
Act

conflict with the
Civil Marriage Act
?

[
10
]

With respect to the
issue of granting a severed judgment for divorce, the following issues will be
addressed:

a.

Does the Court have the
jurisdiction to grant a severed judgment for divorce when the divorce is
contested by one of the parties?

b.

Has Ms. Jewitt
established that the granting of a severed judgment for divorce will result in
prejudice to her such that the Court should not grant the same?

Analysis

[
11
]

The analysis under
s. 15

of the
Charter

has been the subject of numerous Supreme
Court decisions. In
Kahkewistahaw First Nation v Taypotat,
2015 SCC 30
,

[2015] 2 SCR 548
[
Taypotat
]
, the Supreme Court reiterated that the focus
under s. 15 is on whether the law draws discriminatory distinctions which have
the “effect of perpetuating arbitrary disadvantage based on an individual’s
membership in an enumerated or analogous group” (at para. 18; see also
Fraser
v Canada (Attorney General)
,
2020 SCC 28
). This requires the Court to
determine two broad questions:

1.
Does the law, on its face or in its impact,
create a distinction on the basis of an enumerated or analogous ground?

2.    Does the
impugned law fail to respond to the actual capacities and needs of the members
of the group and instead impose a burden or deny a benefit in a manner that has
the effect of reinforcing, perpetuating or exacerbating their disadvantage?

[
12
]

Section 15 ensures
substantive equality. In
Andrews v Law Society of British Columbia
,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1989]
1 SCR 143
[
Andrews
]
, the Supreme Court noted a person “must show not
only that he or she is not receiving equal treatment before and under the law
or that the law has a differential impact on him or her in the protection or
benefit accorded by law but, in addition, must show that the legislative impact
of the law is discriminatory” (at page 182). It is not enough that there is a
distinction. The law must also have a discriminatory impact in terms of
prejudicing or stereotyping. Inherent in the word “distinction” is the idea that
the claimant must be treated differently than others (
Withler v Canada
(Attorney General),
2011 SCC 12
at para
62
,
[2011] 1 SCR 396
). The onus is
on the party alleging the
Charter

violation to prove there has been a
violation of their constitutional rights (
Chaoulli v Quebec (Attorney
General),
2005 SCC 35
at para
30
,
[2005] 1 SCR 791
).

i.        Does granting a civil divorce under the
Divorce Act

discriminate against Ms. Jewitt on the basis of religion, thereby infringing
her rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
?

[
13
]

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter

guarantees that every individual is equal before and under the law and has
the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination based on religion. Ms. Jewitt argues that because her religious
beliefs oppose divorce, granting a divorce in favour of Mr. Van Burgsteden
discriminates against her on the basis of religion and does not uphold the
right to equal protection and benefit of the law as guaranteed by s. 15(1) of
the
Charter.

a.

Distinction
Between Religious and Civil Marriages and Divorces

[
14
]

Ms. Jewitt cites a biblical
passage in relation to the institutional permanence of marriage taken from Matthew
19:6 (King James Version) which provides “What therefore God hath joined
together, let not man put asunder.” She argues the state cannot grant them a
divorce as they are bound by their marriage covenant taken before God. However,
there is a recognized distinction between civil marriages and religious
marriages. The
Divorce Act
gives superior courts the jurisdiction to
dissolve a civil marriage by a divorce judgment. The
Divorce Act
does
not provide a mechanism for the Court to dissolve a marriage in the eyes of God
or to grant a religious divorce. Indeed, as will be discussed below, the
distinction between civil divorces and religious divorces is recognized under

s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
. Further, the biblical passage taken from Matthew
22:21 (King James Version), “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s;
and unto God the things that are God’s,” may be interpreted as recognizing that
members of a society have religious and civil observances for which they may be
responsible and may engage different obligations.

[
15
]

The
Marriage Act, 1836
,
6 & 7 Will IV, c 85 introduced civil marriage as a distinct concept from
religious marriage. Since the concept of civil marriage was introduced, it has
predominated the views of marriage.
However, the distinction between civil and religious
marriage remains and individuals can be married religiously, civilly, or both.
The distinction was explained in 2002 in a paper published by the Department of
Justice Canada, “Marriage and the Legal Recognition of Same-sex Unions: A
Discussion Paper”, ([Ottawa]: Department of Justice, 2002). In that paper, the
Department of Justice explained:

When
individuals marry in a religious ceremony, the legal [civil] and religious
requirements operate together. …

The
distinction between a religious and a civil marriage may be nearly invisible to
many couples getting married in Canada. … Ordinarily, it is the religious
official conducting the wedding ceremony who will take care of the
registration, which then gives the marriage legal recognition. In all cases in
Canada, the religion has the right to perform whatever rites of marriage it
chooses, but the ceremony by itself has no legal consequences unless the
marriage also meets the requirements of federal law and provincial or
territorial law. That is why religious officials must be authorized under
provincial or territorial law to perform ceremonies that are recognized in law.

[
16
]

Ms. Jewitt and Mr. Van
Burgsteden were both religiously and civilly married in a ceremony on August
10, 1991
.
This is expressly recognized by both Virgil D. Anderson and
Ms. Jewitt. Specifically, in his affidavit, Mr. Anderson provides that the
parties were united in marriage “according to the ordinance of God
and
the
laws of Saskatchewan on August 10, 1991” [Emphasis added]. Ms. Jewitt also
recognizes this in her affidavit filed September 3, 2019. By issuing a divorce
judgment pursuant to the
Divorce Act
,
the Court grants a civil divorce.
This civil divorce has no impact on the religious marriage performed according
to the ordinance of God, which is left intact. As a result, granting a civil
divorce does not infringe Ms. Jewitt’s right on the basis of religion under
s.
15(1)
inasmuch as the religious covenant entered into between the parties on
August 10, 1991 is unaffected by a civil divorce.

[
17
]

Numerous cases across
Canada have drawn distinctions between the civil and religious aspects of
marriage. For example,
in
Kanta v Kanta,
2017 BCSC 1428
, the Court
recognized that the parties were religiously married in France in December 2005
but did not civilly marry until March 2006.
In
Silver v Silver,
2017
ONSC 5177
, the Court found that the parties were married in a religious
marriage ceremony in 1991 and were subsequently married in a civil marriage
ceremony in 1996.

[
18
]

In
A.M. v M.S.,
2017
BCSC 2061
, the British Columbia Supreme Court noted that the parties were
married in a dual service involving both a civil marriage and a marriage under
Sharia law. Under the religious marriage, there was a requirement to pay a
mehr,

or dowry. Steeves J. found that the oral agreement between the parties in
relation to the
mehr
dealt with the Iranian religious divorce, and a
separation agreement pertained to their civil divorce. While the parties were
civilly divorced by consent order on March 15, 2016, there had not been a
religious divorce under Sharia law and the issue of the
mehr
was
outstanding. Steeves J. determined the Court does not have jurisdiction over
issues relating to the religious divorce under Sharia law but could
nevertheless compel the parties to follow through on the clear terms of their separation
agreement, including that they would jointly pursue a religious divorce.

[
19
]

In
Davids v David
,

2017 ONSC 895
, the petitioner and the respondent were Orthodox Jews who
believed that marital status was determined religiously by whether or not they
were married by a rabbi. The petitioner had married Mr. David in a civil
ceremony in 2004. She and Mr. David separated in 2006 but did not obtain a
legal divorce. The petitioner and the respondent were subsequently married in a
religious ceremony performed by a rabbi in January 2008. It was irrelevant to
the parties that the petitioner and Mr. David had not been civilly divorced
prior to going through their religious marriage ceremony. They considered
themselves married. In 2012 the respondent terminated the marriage by obtaining
a religious divorce, or “Get” from a rabbi. Although the parties treated their
relationship as a marriage, both acknowledged in their custody dispute over
their children that for legal purposes it was akin to a common law relationship
such that their claims were advanced under
The
Children’s Law Reform Act
,
RSO 1990, c C.12 and not the
Divorce Act
.

[
20
]

The reasons in
Salehi
v Tawoosi,
2016 ONSC 540
[
Salehi
]
, point to the implications for a
breach of the
Charter

which may arise if the Court were to interfere
with the religious aspect of marriage.
In
Salehi
, Myers J. had to
determine whether it was appropriate to compel the respondent husband to provide
the applicant wife with an Islamic Iranian divorce. The parties had been
legally divorced in Canada and the applicant had commenced proceedings in Iran
to compel the respondent to provide her with a religious divorce. Myers J. noted
the provisions of
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
which provides a process
whereby a spouse can file an affidavit with prescribed contents concerning
religious barriers to divorce. On the filing of such an affidavit, s. 21.1(3)
empowers the Court to provide specific procedural relief in relation to the
divorce proceeding in Canada, including the striking of pleadings. Myers J. concluded
that the issue of a “religious divorce” was better left to the Iranian proceedings
given the applicant had already commenced proceedings in Iran for that relief.

[
21
]

Myers J. noted there
was a distinction between striking pleadings to try to encourage or coerce a
religious divorce under
s. 21.1
of the
Divorce Act
, and the making of a
mandatory injunction whereby a government official positively compels a party to
perform a religious act. Myers J. determined that “to order a person to do a
religious act - implicates issues of freedom of religion under the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
”. Further, he pointed to
s. 21.1(4)
of the
Divorce
Act
which contains a defence to an application under ss. (3) where the
respondent proves that he has a genuine religious issue. Without deciding the
issue, Myers J. suggested that the relief that the Court may grant under s.
21.1 of the
Divorce Act
did not extend to the granting of a mandatory
injunction to compel a person to grant a religious divorce as the same may
infringe the
Charter
.

[
22
]

The division between
religious and civil marriages can also protect the right to freedom of religion
under the
Charter

in some circumstances. In
Marriage Commissioners
Appointed Under the Marriage Act (Re),
2011 SKCA 3
,
327 DLR (4th) 669
, the
Court held that
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
protects not only the right to
freely exercise one’s religion but also the right to be free from compulsion to
practice or recognize any religion. Under the scheme of the
Marriage Act, 1995
,
SS 1995, c M‑4.1, the solemnization of marriage “by a marriage
commissioner is provided as a non-religious alternative for those who, for any
reason, are unable to have their marriage solemnized by clergy, or who choose
not to do so” (at para. 121). In essence, there must be a distinction between
civil and religious marriages because people have a right to be free from
compulsion to practice or recognize a religion. If non-religious individuals
were launched into a sacrament of God through any type of marriage ceremony
when such sacrament is not in accordance with their religious beliefs, it would
violate their right to freedom of religion.

[
23
]

A similar sentiment was

expressed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bruker v Marcovitz,
2007 SCC
54
,
[2007] 3 SCR 607
[
Bruker
]
, a case where the applicant wife was
seeking to enforce the terms of a separation agreement under which the husband
had agreed to cooperate in obtaining a “Get”, a Jewish divorce which only the
husband can give. The wife cannot obtain a “Get” unless her husband agrees to
release his wife from marriage and authorizes her to remarry. This process
takes place before a rabbi. When the husband does not voluntarily give the
“Get,” his wife is without religious recourse and retains the status of “wife”
pursuant to the Jewish religion. At para. 5, Abella J. for a majority of the
Court identified the practical and personal implications that arise out of the
distinction, here for a Jewish woman, between a civil and religious divorce:

[5] For an observant Jewish woman in Canada, this presents a
dichotomous scenario: under Canadian law, she is free to divorce her husband
regardless of his consent; under Jewish law, however, she remains married to
him unless he gives his consent.  This means that while she can remarry under
Canadian law, she is prevented from remarrying in accordance with her
religion.  The inability to do so, for many Jewish women, results in the loss
of their ability to remarry at all.

[
24
]

The Court outlined that
the ramifications of the situation extended to any children she would have upon
civil remarriage who would be considered “illegitimate” under Jewish law.

[
25
]

These cases illustrate that
in Canada the civil divorce process has no bearing or impact on religious
marriages and divorces. Just because an individual obtains a civil divorce and
can remarry legally under Canadian law does not necessarily mean that the
individual is free to remarry religiously. As such, a civil divorce cannot
infringe freedom of religion under the
Charter

or discriminate on the
basis of religion

because under Canadian law it has no impact on the
religious marriage between the parties. Secular courts are incapable of
granting a religious divorce because doing so would, in the words of
Iacobucci
J., “
unjustifiably
entangle the court in the affairs of religion” (
Syndicat Northcrest v
Amselem
,
2004 SCC 47
at para
50
,
[2004] 2 SCR 551
)
. If a civil divorce is granted in this
case, the parties will remain religiously united, absent a religious dissolution
of marriage. The evidence of Ms. Jewitt and her pastor, Mr. Anderson,
confirm the same.

[
26
]

Finally, as
the decision
in
Bruker
demonstrates, even if Ms. Jewitt could identify an impairment
to religious freedom in these circumstances, such impairment would be significantly
outweighed by the harm both to Mr. Van Burgsteden and to the public’s interest
in protecting fundamental values such as equality rights and autonomous choice
in marriage and divorce [
Bruker
, paras
71 to 80]
.

[
27
]

Accordingly, Ms.
Jewitt’s constitutional challenge in relation to equal protection based on
religious beliefs is dismissed.

b.

Is the
Divorce Act

discriminatory
on the basis of religion under
s. 15(1)
?

[
28
]

Despite having disposed
of this argument in the preceding section because religion is not engaged in
the civil divorce process, I will nonetheless proceed to determine whether the
Divorce
Act

discriminates against Ms. Jewitt on religious grounds under
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
.

[
29
]

The first question to
be determined under the s. 15 analysis in relation to this case is to determine
whether the
Divorce Act
,
on its face or in its impact, creates a
distinction on the basis of Ms. Jewitt’s religious beliefs. There is none. A
civil divorce does not dissolve the religious marriage. Provided that the
grounds for divorce under the
Divorce Act
exist, everyone is entitled to
a civil divorce. Regardless of whether the parties have a particular religious
belief or not, the criteria to obtain a divorce are the same, applied equally
to all.

[
30
]

The
Divorce Act

does
not force parties to obtain a
religious
divorce which is against their
religion. The
Divorce Act
deals only with the civil marriage contract
and the dissolution thereof.  In the context of this case,
if
Ms. Jewitt
and Mr. Van Burgsteden both agreed that a civil divorce was not permitted by
their religion, there is nothing in the
Divorce Act
that forces them to
obtain a divorce. However, as argued by counsel for Mr. Van Burgsteden, denying
him a civil divorce because of Ms. Jewitt’s opposition based on her religious
beliefs would violate his right to freedom of religion. It would force Ms.
Jewitt’s religious beliefs onto Mr. Van Burgsteden and deny him a right to
which he is civilly entitled.

[
31
]

In enacting
s. 21.1
of
the
Divorce Act
, Parliament has recognized the importance of parties
being able to obtain a civil divorce from their spouse and being able to take
procedural steps to encourage an eventual religious divorce, subject to the
overriding defence under
s. 21.1(4)
that the spouse has genuine grounds of a
religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the barriers to a
religious divorce (
Bruker
, paras
80 to 82
). Neither party has raised an
issue here of seeking a religious divorce or of the other creating a barrier to
obtaining a religious divorce.

[
32
]

Having established that
there is no distinction on the basis of an enumerated or analogous ground, it
is unnecessary to proceed to the next step of the analysis, being the
determination of whether the distinction creates a disadvantage. If, however, I
had found that there was a distinction on the basis of religion, Ms. Jewitt has
not provided sufficient evidence to establish that the distinction
discriminates against the group to which she belongs, being Evangelical
Lutherans, due to their religious beliefs. Given that Ms. Jewitt has the onus
of demonstrating the
Charter

violation, the lack of evidence would be
fatal to her claim. Regardless, there can be no disadvantage caused to
Evangelical Lutherans because civil divorce does not interfere with religious
marriage. For these reasons, the
Divorce Act

does not violate the
s. 15(1)

right to equal protection and benefit of the law on the basis of religion.

ii.         Does granting a civil divorce under the
Divorce Act

discriminate against Ms. Jewitt on the basis of mental disability, thereby
infringing her rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
?

[
33
]

Section 15(1)
of the
Charter

guarantees that every individual is equal before and under the law and has
the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination based on mental or physical disability. Ms. Jewitt claims that
granting a divorce under the
Divorce Act

will further contribute to the
deterioration of her mental health. As a result, she claims that granting a
divorce would violate her right to equal protection under the law based on
mental disability.

[
34
]

Ms. Jewitt has the
burden of proving that the
Divorce Act

disproportionately affects the
group or individual based on membership in an enumerated or analogous ground.
She has failed to adduce the necessary evidence to establish differential
treatment based on the enumerated ground of mental disability.

[
35
]

First, it is clear that
the
Divorce Act

does not draw a formal distinction based on mental
disability. Regardless of an individual’s mental status, if the criteria for
divorce are established, superior courts may grant a divorce.

[
36
]

However, even where a
law does not draw a formal distinction on the basis of an enumerated or
analogous ground, it can nonetheless constitute discrimination under
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
.
In
Eldridge v British Columbia (Attorney General),
1997 CanLII 327 (SCC)
,
[1997]
3 SCR 624
,

the Supreme Court explained the distinction between direct
and adverse effect discrimination in the context of health care service
provisions for deaf individuals:

77      This Court has
consistently held, then, that discrimination can arise both from the adverse
effects of rules of general application as well as from express
distinctions flowing from the distribution of benefits. Given this state of
affairs, I can think of no principled reason why it should not be possible to
establish a claim of discrimination based on the adverse effects of a facially
neutral benefit scheme.
Section 15(1)
expressly states, after all, that
every individual is “equal before and under the law and has the right to the
equal protection
and
equal benefit of the law without
discrimination...” (emphasis added). The provision makes no distinction between
laws that impose unequal burdens and those that deny equal benefits. …

[
37
]

Additionally,
in
Adler
v Ontario,
1996 CanLII 148 (SCC)
,
[1996] 3 SCR 609
, the Supreme Court, citing Peter W. Hogg,
Constitutional
Law of Canada
,

looseleaf 3d ed, vol 2 (Scarborough: Carswell, 1992),
stated that it is “a necessary corollary of the rule that discrimination may be
indirect and unintended that a law may have to make reasonable accommodation
for those who, by reason of religious affiliation or disability (for example),
are discriminated against by otherwise neutral laws.”

[
38
]

As cited by the
Attorney General in its Brief of Law,
in
Taypotat
,
the Supreme Court commented
on the importance of having an evidentiary basis to support a claim for adverse
effects discrimination under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
In that case, the
constitutionality of an Election Code which provided that candidates who wished
to run for chief or a band councillor had to have a grade 12 education was
challenged. The Court concluded that the case failed based “on the absence of
any evidence linking the requirement to a disparate impact on members of an
enumerated or analogous group” (at para. 15).

[
39
]

When establishing that
a law has a disproportionate effect on the claimant based on his or her
membership in an enumerated or analogous ground, the evidentiary burden will
vary depending on the circumstances (
Taypotat

at para
21
). While census
data may be useful, it is not required.
The Supreme Court in
Taypotat

held that “[w]hile the evidentiary burden need not be onerous, the evidence
must amount to more than a web of instinct” (at para. 34).

[
40
]

Ms. Jewitt has not
presented any evidence to establish that the effect of the
Divorce Act

has
a disproportionate impact on individuals with mental disabilities; it is not
clear what impact civil divorce has on people with mental disabilities. The
only evidence that Ms. Jewitt presented is in affidavit form and provides that
she herself believes that a divorce under the
Divorce Act
will
exacerbate her already fragile mental state. However, based on
the reasoning in

Taypotat
,
that is insufficient to demonstrate a distinction based on
mental disability. As such, I am unable to conclude that the
Divorce Act
draws
a distinction or has the effect of creating a distinction on Ms. Jewitt on the
basis of her being a member of the group to which she belongs, being mental
disability.

[
41
]

Even if Ms. Jewitt had established
that the
Divorce Act

disproportionately impacts individuals with mental
disabilities, I would be unable to conclude that the
Divorce Act
is
discriminatory. Again, Ms. Jewitt bears the burden of proving that the
disproportionate impact of the
Divorce Act
has the effect of
discriminating against individuals with mental disabilities. She has not
provided a sufficient evidentiary basis to establish that the
Divorce Act
imposes
a burden or denies a benefit in a manner that has the effect of reinforcing,
perpetuating or exacerbating disadvantage.

iii.
If Ms. Jewitt’s
s. 15(1)

Charter

rights are infringed, are the infringements saved by
s. 1
?

[
42
]

Had I found a violation
of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter

on the basis of Ms. Jewitt’s belonging
to the enumerated group of religion or mental disability or both, the
infringement would be saved under
s. 1
of the
Charter.
The Supreme Court
set out the test for a determination under s. 1 of the
Charter
in
R v
Oakes
,

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
,
[1986] 1 SCR 103
.
The party seeking to uphold the
impugned law has the burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that:

(1)

the objective of the
law is pressing and substantial; and

(2)

the means chosen to
achieve the objective are reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society. This requires:

a.

the rights violation to
be rationally connected to the objective of the law;

b.   the impugned law to minimally impair
the
Charter

guarantee; and

c.   proportionality between the effect of
the law and its objective so that the attainment of the objective is not
outweighed by the abridgment of the right.

[
43
]

I find that the
objective of the
Divorce Act

is pressing and substantial. The purpose of
the
Divorce Act
is to stipulate a framework for the dissolution of
marriages and provide a mechanism for parties to obtain corollary relief when a
civil divorce is granted. The ability to grant a divorce and order corollary
relief is integral to the functioning of society when a marriage has broken
down and there is no possibility of reconciliation. There is an appropriate
balance to be struck between upholding the sanctity of marriage and the
public’s interest in dissolving unions that have broken down. The
Divorce
Act
seeks to achieve that balance.

[
44
]

Additionally, the means
chosen by the legislature in enacting the
Divorce Act

achieve the
objective and are reasonably and demonstrably justified. The rights violations,
if they were established, are rationally connected to the objective of
dissolving civil marriages where there is no possibility of reconciliation.
They provide a mechanism for the dissolution of the marriage when certain
statutory criteria are met.

[
45
]

The
Divorce Act

is
also minimally impairing.  The
Divorce Act
legislates only the civil
aspect of marriage and does not delve into the religious beliefs of any of the
parties. Additionally, different religions have differing beliefs on the
appropriateness of divorce. Therefore, it would be nearly impossible for the
legislature to craft a legislative regime that recognizes the individualized
impacts and effects of divorce. By only dissolving civil marriages and by
granting divorces only when certain criteria have been met, the
Divorce Act
is
minimally impairing.

[
46
]

Further, the
Divorce
Act

cannot reasonably accommodate every type of mental disability which may
be negatively or positively impacted by the divorce process. To require the
legislature to take into account the varying degrees of mental disability and
numerous religious beliefs to craft solutions to further minimize the impact of
divorce would be unduly onerous. Every individual who suffers from a mental
disability may be impacted differently from the divorce process; some may even
benefit from the dissolution of a broken-down civil marriage. However, the
Divorce
Act
balances these and other economic advantages and disadvantages that
spouses incur on marriage breakdown and divorce through the corollary relief
provisions under the
Divorce Act
, including spousal support. As noted,
Ms. Jewitt has included a claim for spousal support in her counter-petition in
this proceeding.

[
47
]

Finally, the
Divorce
Act

is proportionate in that the benefits of the
Divorce Act
are not
outweighed by the negative costs of the rights limitation. Divorce is a
necessary and important legislative response to the breakdown of civil
marriages. The
Divorce Act
provides a structured mechanism for parties
to obtain a divorce and corollary relief when a marriage has broken down and
there is no possibility of reconciliation. The potential negative impacts
claimed by Ms. Jewitt do not outweigh this integral objective.

iv.
If the
infringements are not saved under s. 1, what is the appropriate
remedy?

[
48
]

Given that Ms. Jewitt
has failed to establish an infringement of her
Charter

rights and any infringement would be saved under
s. 1
of the
Charter,
it is unnecessary to consider an appropriate remedy.
However, I do note that the remedy requested by Ms. Jewitt is likely not
available. Ms. Jewitt is not asking this Court to declare the
Divorce Act

unconstitutional and strike down the legislation or
impugned provisions. Instead, she is asking the Court to decline to grant a
divorce between her and Mr. Van Burgsteden as an individual remedy.

[
49
]

Section 52
of the
Constitution Act, 1982

does not allow a court to provide
individualized remedies when a law is found to be unconstitutional in that it
violates a right or freedom guaranteed under the
Charter.
Section 52
provides that any law that is inconsistent with the provisions
of the Constitution, to the extent of the inconsistency, are of no force and
effect. That being said,
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
grants the Court broad remedial powers to grant a remedy that the Court
considers appropriate and just in the circumstances.

[
50
]

If the
Divorce Act

was found to violate constitutional guarantees under

s. 15(1)
by making divorce available as argued by Ms. Jewitt, the impugned
provisions of the
Divorce
Act
would need to be
struck down and declared of no force and effect. It would be inappropriate and
unjust for this Court to provide an individualized remedy for Ms. Jewitt in
these circumstances if the legislative regime was found to be unconstitutional.

v.         Does
the
Divorce Act

conflict with the preamble of the
Constitution Act,
1982
,
rendering it inoperable?

[
51
]

Ms. Jewitt argues that
because the preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1982

provides that “Canada
is founded upon the principles that recognize the supremacy of God,” the
Divorce
Act

is inconsistent with the
Constitution Act, 1982
. She argues that
since the marriage between her and Mr. Van Burgsteden was performed in
accordance with the ordinance of God, it is a permanent institution severable
only by death. As a result, she claims that “dissolution of the union of
marriage performed in accordance with the ordinance of God is not permissible”
under the
Divorce Act.
Presumably, she seeks a remedy under
s. 52
of the

Constitution Act, 1982
which provides that any law that is inconsistent
with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency,
of no force and effect.

[
52
]

The preamble’s reference
to the supremacy of God has been judicially considered on multiple occasions.
In
O’Sullivan v Canada,
1991 CanLII 13582 (FC)
,
[1992] 1 FC 522 (Fed Ct)
,  the Federal Court
considered the phrase “supremacy of God.” At para. 19, the Court noted:

[19]    The preamble to the
Charter

provides an important
element in defining Canada, but recognition of the supremacy of God, emplaced
in the supreme law of Canada, goes no further than this: it prevents the
Canadian state from becoming officially atheistic. It does not make Canada a theocracy
because of the enormous variety of beliefs of how God (apparently the very same
deity for Jews, Christians and Muslims) wants people to behave generally and to
worship in particular. The preamble’s recognition of the supremacy of God,
then, does not prevent Canada from being a secular state.

[
53
]

In
Pappas v The
Queen,
2006 TCC 692
, Mr. Pappas argued that it was unconstitutional to
force citizens to pay taxes as it was sinful in the eyes of God. He argued that
he had no freedom of choice in whether to pay taxes and as a result, he could
not exercise his “God given right of free will as guaranteed” through the
“supremacy of God and the observance of God’s Law.” At para. 9, the Tax Court
of Canada held:

[9]        … His allegations that the legislation is contrary to the
Charter

stem from a conviction that the
Charter,
by its preamble that Canada
is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God, is subject to
certain biblical scriptures. In this regard, he argues that it is sinful in the
eyes of God to be a tax collector; therefore, any legislation forcing citizens
to be such is contrary to the
Charter.
I do not accept Mr. Pappas’
argument.
An introductory statement in the
Charter
recognizing Canada
is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God is not an
invitation to superimpose passages from the Bible onto the country’s
legislation.
This would create at best, confusion, and at worst, chaos. Mr.
Pappas is attempting to elevate the
Charter
preamble to the status of an
overriding statement of law akin to a specific section of the legislation. He
is in effect arguing there is a higher law, the law of God, which is being
breached by provisions of the
Excise Tax Act.

That law, he
suggests, is incorporated into our
Charter.
With respect, it is not.
[Emphasis added]

[
54
]

The Supreme Court also
considered the reference to the supremacy of God in the preamble in
Mouvement
laique québécois v Saguenay (City),
2015 SCC 16
,
[2015] 2 SCR 3
. At para. 147,
the Court clarifies that the reference to the supremacy of God articulates the
political theory on which the
Charter
’s

protections are based but
cannot be relied upon to reduce the scope of a guarantee that is expressly
provided for in the
Charter
.

Moreover, the Court quoted from “The
‘Supremacy of God’, Human Dignity and the
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
”
(2003), 52 UNBLJ 227 at 229, where Professor L. Sossin explained as follows:

The
reference to the supremacy of God in the
Charter

should not be construed
so as to suggest one religion is favoured over another in Canada, nor that
monotheism is more desirable than polytheism, nor that the God-fearing are
entitled to greater rights and privileges than atheists or agnostics.
Any
of these interpretations would be at odds with the purpose and orientation of
the
Charter,
as well as with the specific provisions regarding freedom
of religion and conscience under
s. 2
. [Emphasis added]

[
55
]

What can be gleaned
from the aforementioned passages is that the phrase “supremacy of God” in the
preamble does not incorporate God’s law into the laws of Canada. As a result,
the fact that the Bible recognizes the sanctity of marriage and, in Ms.
Jewitt’s view, opposes divorce, does not mean that Canadian law must abide by
those beliefs. To interpret the reference to the “supremacy of God” in a manner
that would incorporate Ms. Jewitt’s religious beliefs into Canadian law would
favour one religion over others and as Professor Sossin identifies “would be at
odds with the purpose and orientation of the
Charter
”. As a result, the
provisions of the
Divorce Act

that allow for the dissolution of civil
marriages do not conflict with the preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

vi.        Does the
Divorce Act

conflict with
the
Civil Marriage Act
?

[
56
]

Ms. Jewitt opposes the
grant of a divorce under the
Divorce Act

on the ground that it conflicts
with the
Civil Marriage Act
,
which recognizes marriage as “a fundamental
institution in Canadian Society.” She further points to the fact that the
Civil
Marriage Act
indicates that the Parliament of Canada has a responsibility
to support the institution of marriage “because it strengthens commitment in
relationships and represents the foundation of family life for many Canadians.”
She argues that dissolution of marriage under the
Divorce Act
is in
direct opposition to the premise found in the
Civil Marriage Act
as it
undermines the institution of marriage and the foundation of family life.

[
57
]

The context of the
Civil
Marriage Act

is important. The
Act
was introduced to extend the
availability of the institution of marriage to same-sex couples and explained
why the government was doing so. It also made amendments to the
Divorce Act

so
that same-sex couples had equal access to divorce. As a result, while Parliament
saw the importance of allowing same-sex couples to legally marry civilly, it
also recognized that same-sex couples may also need access to legal civil
divorces. The
Act
has no bearing on the availability of divorce in
Canada, nor on the principles in which divorce should or should not be granted.

Conclusion on Constitutional Issues

[
58
]

Based on the above
analysis, I find that the
Divorce Act

does not infringe Ms. Jewitt’s
constitutional rights as claimed. She has been unable to establish that the
Divorce
Act
disproportionately affects and discriminates against her on the basis
of her membership to the Evangelical Lutheran faith, or on the basis of her
mental disability. Additionally, the
Divorce Act
does not conflict with
the preamble of the
Charter
,
or the
Civil Marriage Act
.
Ms.
Jewitt’s applications challenging the constitutionality of the
Divorce Act

are therefore dismissed.

Severance of Divorce Proceeding

[
59
]

As outlined above, Mr.
Van Burgsteden seeks to have the divorce proceeding severed from the parties’
corollary relief and family property proceedings. Mr. Van Burgsteden has
established the requisite criteria entitling him to a divorce including
residency, separation in excess of one year, the absence of collusion and no
possibility of reconciliation. He is living with another woman in a spousal
relationship. They want to get married. Mr. Van Burgsteden argues Ms. Jewitt is
unnecessarily delaying the proceedings between the parties, including avoiding
service of process which resulted in an application to validate service upon
her and subsequently not following through on providing financial disclosure
such that the support and property claims can be dealt with.

[
60
]

Ms. Jewitt opposes the
severance of the divorce judgment from the property division and spousal
support issues on the basis of financial, professional and psychological
prejudice. First, she argues the Court cannot grant severance other than in
circumstances where the divorce is consensual. Second, she opposes the granting
of the divorce on religious and moral grounds, suggesting there is a
possibility of reconciliation between the parties. Third, she argues the
granting of a severed judgment for divorce will prejudicially affect her legal
rights in this proceeding. She prognosticates that if a divorce were granted
and Mr. Van Burgsteden died suddenly, she would be unable to obtain spousal maintenance
against his estate and therefore, there is a potential for economic prejudice
to her. Further, she is concerned the granting of a divorce will exacerbate her
mental health issues. Finally, she cites numerous cases that she alleges stand
for the proposition that severance will not be granted in the absence of urgent
or compelling reasons on behalf of the petitioner if there is a risk of
prejudice to the respondent spouse.

[
61
]

Ms. Jewitt also argued
that the Court could not grant severance of the divorce judgment given her
constitutional challenge to the
Divorce Act
, inasmuch as the granting of
the divorce would be prejudicial to the same. As I have dismissed her
constitutional challenge, this argument no longer has any merit.

[
62
]

As outlined above the
following issues will be addressed:

a.

Does the Court have the
jurisdiction to grant a severed judgment for divorce when the divorce is
contested by one of the parties?

b.

Has Ms. Jewitt
established that the granting of a severed judgment for divorce will result in
prejudice to her such that the Court should not grant the same?

Analysis

Legal Principles

[
63
]

The
Divorce Act

and

The Queen’s Bench Rules
provide for the severance of divorce proceedings
from other claims raised by the parties. Provided the requirements of
s. 8
of
the
Divorce Act
have been met to grant the divorce and there are no bars
to divorce as set out in
s. 11
of the
Divorce Act
the Court has the
jurisdiction to grant a divorce. Even though a judgment for divorce may be
granted, the
Divorce Act
allows for corollary relief proceedings to be continued
or brought by former spouses. Thus, severing the granting of the judgment for
divorce from other relief sought is contemplated by the
Divorce Act
, given
the jurisdiction of the Court to grant corollary relief between former spouses.

[
64
]

Rule 15-43 of
The
Queen’s Bench Rules
grants the Court discretion to sever a divorce judgment
from other matters in a family law proceeding. Specifically, Rule 15-43
provides, in part:

15-43(1) A judgment in a divorce proceeding
must be in Form 15-43.

(2) If the Court makes an order granting
child support, a separate formal order embodying the child support must be
issued.

(3) If a claim for divorce is made
together with one or more other claims, the Court may:

(a)  grant a divorce and direct that a judgment
of divorce alone be entered; and

(b)  either:

(i) adjourn the hearing of the other claims; or

(ii) give judgment on the other claims.

…

[
65
]

Ms. Jewitt recognizes
the Court has the discretion to grant a severed divorce, however, she argues the
exercise of that discretion is dependent on the parties consenting to the same,
there being a compelling reason to grant the divorce and there being no
prejudice to a party by the granting of the same.

(a)       Does
the Court have the jurisdiction to grant a severed judgment for divorce when
the divorce is contested by one of the parties?

[
66
]

The issue of severance
has been considered by Saskatchewan courts on multiple occasions.
In
Rimmer
v Adshead,
2002 SKCA 12
,
[2002] 4 WWR 119
[
Rimmer
]
, the petitioner
obtained a divorce by means of a default judgment. Shortly after the divorce
was finalized, the respondent sought to have the proceedings reopened and
applied for distribution of family property and spousal support. When hearing
the appeal, the Court of Appeal made the following comments on severance at
para. 37:

[37]
… In divorce and related proceedings, the court often severs the divorce proceeding,
if the divorce be uncontested, from the proceedings for corollary and other
relief and then grants judgment for divorce, leaving the claims for corollary
and other relief to be determined later. Once determined, the results are then
incorporated into the judgment. …

[
67
]

In
Behnami v
Mirakhori
,
2013 SKQB 177
,
420 Sask R 197
[
Behnami
]
, Wilkinson J.
addressed the issue of severance. The central question in that case was whether
the husband’s family property claim would be prejudiced by severing the issues
and granting a divorce. Wilkinson J. concluded that granting a divorce would
have little impact on the division of family property. In deciding the matter,
she succinctly distilled the test to be applied on a severance application with
reference to
Rimmer
at para
15
as follows:

[15]  The
Court of Appeal commented that such power is discretionary and therefore falls
to be exercised as the judge, acting judicially, thinks fit, having regard for
considerations such as the impact of delay in granting the relief, and whether
any party will suffer prejudice or irreparable harm.

[
68
]

In
Yung v Yung,
2006
SKQB 388
,
284 Sask R 10
[
Yung
]
,
Sandomirsky J. commented on the
need for reasons to be given as to why severance is necessary or desirable. In
that context, he held as follows at para. 5:

[5]   Clearly, a severed divorce judgment cannot be granted without
proof that reasonable provision has been made for the support of any children
of the marriage —
s. 11(1)
(b) of the
Divorce Act
. Second, it is
necessary, in my opinion, to provide by way of affidavit evidence, sufficient
reason or reasons as to why severance is necessary or desirable. An order for
severance cannot be granted in the absence of such evidence. Those reasons may
involve moral or religious reasons, medical reasons, legal factors or general
public/social policy considerations. But, at a minimum, there must be a genuine
reason for an order for severance to be requested. Therefore, in the event of a
genuine and substantive reason, where the evidence establishes grounds for
divorce,
and, where the respondent does not reasonably oppose the granting
of a severed judgment for divorce, such a request should be granted
. When a
marriage has failed and there has been sufficient passage of time to discount
the reasonable prospect of reconciliation, a spouse or the spouses deserve the
right of closure and the right to move forward in their respective lives free
of the restrictions of a defunct marriage. The parties, and indeed their legal
counsel, must always address the legal implications which may flow from the
dissolution of the marriage. The spouses must be aware of any negative legal
consequence to the granting of divorce before making an application for a
severed divorce.

[Emphasis added]

[
69
]

Ms. Jewitt argues that
Rimmer

and
Yung
stand for the proposition that a “condition” of severance
is that the parties must consent to the divorce, or not oppose the same. I do
not agree. Neither case expressly precludes severance where one of the parties
opposes the divorce.

[
70
]

Even though the passage
from
Rimmer,
quoted above, suggests severance is a common occurrence in
the context of
uncontested divorces
, the Court does not expressly
preclude the ability to sever when the divorce is contested.  The Court went on
to outline that the jurisdiction to sever divorce proceedings from corollary
issues is inherently discretionary. As long as a judge does not abuse his or
her discretion, err in principle, disregard a material matter of fact or fail
to act judicially, the decision to exercise discretion to sever is appropriate,
provided that the result is not so plainly wrong “as to amount to an injustice
and invite intervention on that basis” (
Rimmer

at para
58
).

[
71
]

In identifying the need
for there to be
reasonable opposition
, Sandomirsky J.
in
Yung
was
not saying that mere lack of consent to the application by one party would
suffice to prevent the Court from exercising its discretion to grant a severed divorce
judgment in appropriate circumstances. Rather, the Court should consider the
reasonableness of any opposition to the granting of a severed judgment for
divorce and judiciously exercise its discretion in granting or rejecting the
application on the evidence.

[
72
]

Further, Sandomirsky J.
did not identify that the evidence before the Court needed to be “compelling”
before the Court could exercise its discretion. Rather, he indicated the evidence
needed to establish a genuine and substantive reason for granting a severed
judgment for divorce, while highlighting that the parties and counsel needed to
be mindful of possible negative consequences to the granting of a severed
judgment for divorce. In that context, he encouraged the filing of evidence “as
to why severance is necessary or desirable”. He provided some insight into the
types of grounds for which a severed judgment for divorce may be sought,
including “moral or religious reasons, medical reasons, legal factors or
general public/social policy considerations.” However, as I
noted in
Theriault
v Theriault
,
2014 SKQB 423
,
461 Sask R 221
[
Theriault
]
, when deciding
whether to sever a divorce from corollary issues, there is no closed list of
considerations that the Court is to have regard for. Each case is to be
determined on its own facts.

[
73
]

In
Theriault
, the petitioner applied to sever the
divorce judgment from the corollary relief issues where the respondent had
subsequently brought proceedings for divorce in Japan. The respondent opposed
the application for two reasons. First, he argued that the Court should
withhold pronouncing a divorce until the court in Japan had determined whether
it would exercise jurisdiction in the matter. Secondly, he claimed that
severing the divorce judgment from the other claims would cause him undue
prejudice given Japan did not have an equivalent system of spousal support payable
to an ex-spouse and inclusion/deduction income tax rules had no application.

[
74
]

In a prior
decision of
this Court,
2014 SKQB 373
, Wilson J. had already determined that the
Saskatchewan Court had jurisdiction to decide the matters in dispute between the
parties. I rejected the husband’s argument that severing and granting the
divorce would cause him prejudice either with respect to the different tax
treatment of spousal support under the Canadian tax regime versus the Japanese
tax regime or regarding issues of juridical advantage. Finally, I concluded that
delaying the divorce judgment would encourage a multiplicity of proceedings and
granting the divorce would crystalize the Court’s jurisdiction over the
matters. As a result, the divorce judgment was granted and the remaining issues
between the parties pertaining to family property division and spousal support
were adjourned.

[
75
]

Courts in other
jurisdictions have granted severed judgments for divorce in contested
circumstances.

[
76
]

In a factually similar case
to the circumstances here,
Winstanley v Winstanley,
2009 MBQB 41
,
237
Man R (2d) 182

[
Winstanley
]
, the wife moved for an order severing
the divorce from other matters in issue, including family property division.
While the husband did not oppose the divorce entirely, he argued that the
proceedings should be adjourned pending efforts to reconcile. Carr J. held that
while severance is not “a matter of right,” when divorce is no way tied to
other relief claimed and reconciliation is not possible, there is no reason to
withhold the divorce judgment. The resistance to the severance application was
found to be an “attempt to starve the wife into reconciling” (at para. 13).

[
77
]

In
Pires v Pires,
2005
CarswellBC 3358 (WL)
(BCSC) [
Pires
]
, Mr. Pires opposed the application
for divorce on religious grounds. Mr. Pires was a devout Catholic and insisted
that there was a possibility of reconciliation. The Court concluded that Ms. Pires
had resolutely and consistently denied that reconciliation was a possibility.
As a result, there was no possibility of reconciliation and the Court granted
the divorce despite the husband’s opposition. The Court of Appeal upheld that
ruling
in
Pires v Pires,
2006 BCCA 137
, again noting that Mr. Pires
opposed the divorce on the basis of religious grounds. It was clear to the
Court of Appeal that there was no possibility of reconciliation due to Ms.
Pire’s opposition to any and all reconciliation efforts.

[
78
]

Ms. Jewitt advanced a
comparable argument to the one advanced
in
Pires
suggesting there was a possibility
of reconciliation with Mr. Van Burgsteden, despite his evidence to the contrary.
She claims that “no individual or organization is able to predict the future.
There are many instances where spouses are divorced and then remarry each other.
The Court therefore cannot reasonably comment on the permanence of marital
breakdown based solely on the present circumstances before it.” Ms. Jewitt’s
argument relates to
s. 10
of the
Divorce Act
which requires the Court to
adjourn a divorce proceeding at any stage, “where it appears to the court from
the nature of the case, the evidence or the attitude of either or both spouses
that there is a possibility of reconciliation of the spouses”.

[
79
]

In
Pires
, counsel
for the husband, who opposed the granting of the divorce, argued
s. 10
of the
Divorce
Act
required the Court to adjourn a divorce proceeding where there was any
possibility of reconciliation regardless of how remote and even if one party is
opposed. The British Columbia Court of Appeal rejected that argument. The Court
determined that the wording of the section required the Court to consider the
evidence regarding the possibility of reconciliation. In pointing to the
wording of s. 10, the Court identified that the task of the judge was to determine
whether in all the circumstances reconciliation was possible. A mere
possibility of reconciliation would not therefore suffice to prevent the Court
from exercising its discretion to grant a severed judgment for divorce.

[
80
]

Section 10 does not
include any words qualifying the word “possible” as it relates to the prospect
of reconciliation. Nevertheless, I prefer the reasoning of Carr  J.
in
Winstanley
.
There, Carr J. held
s. 10
of the
Divorce Act

should be interpreted as
requiring that there is no
realistic
possibility of reconciliation. As
he pointed out at para. 3: “Almost anything is possible! As there exists
no realistic possibility that these parties will reconcile, the application to
adjourn is dismissed.” The same can be said about this case. While it is true
that the Court cannot comment on the permanence of marital breakdown with any
degree of certainty, there is no realistic possibility of reconciliation in the
foreseeable future where attempts at counselling have failed and Mr. Van
Burgsteden has made it clear in his affidavit evidence he has no interest in
reconciling. Further, since the parties’ separation he has involved himself in
a spousal relationship with another woman whom he now seeks to marry. These are
not circumstances in which reconciliation is possible.

[
81
]

I have already
addressed from a constitutionality perspective Ms. Jewitt’s opposition on
religious grounds to the divorce judgment being granted. Much of my reasoning
with respect to the distinction between civil and religious aspects of marriage
and the implications of a civil divorce to religious marriages can be applied
here. Religious opposition to a civil divorce is often rejected by the Court as
a ground for not granting a severed divorce judgment.

[
82
]

For example,
in
Qually
v Qually

(1987)
,
1987 CanLII 4775 (SK QB)
,
56 Sask R 165 (QB)
, the husband responded to the
wife’s petition for divorce by challenging the constitutionality of the
Divorce
Act
.
Specifically, he argued that marital status was a fundamental right
and that the Court’s ability to issue a divorce judgment after the parties had
lived separate and apart for only one year was not in accordance with the
principles of fundamental justice. Dickson J. rejected that argument and made
the following comments at page 171:

Apart from
the authorities cited, it seems to me that labeling marriage status and family
life as “rights” does violence to the English language. Marriage status is no
more than a description of a person’s relation to another. It is simply a
social position recognized by the law. It emanates from the choice of two
persons, both of whom wish to have a legal relationship with the other. How can
only one of those persons claim a right to enter or maintain that relationship
with the other? Family life is no more than a description of the daily activity
of two or more persons who have chosen to live together. How can one person
claim a right to an activity that, by its very nature, requires the consent by
all who participate? …

[
83
]

This ruling was upheld
by the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal (
Qually v Qually
,
1988 CanLII 5385 (SK CA)
,
[1989] 2 WWR 268
(Sask CA)
).

[
84
]

Baxter v Baxter
(1983),
1983 CanLII 1801 (ON HCJ)
,
45 OR (2d) 348 (Ont H Ct)
, also
provides
useful guidance. In that case, the respondent argued that a decree
nisi

should not be made absolute. He claimed that a decree absolute would infringe
his rights to freedom of religion as guaranteed under
s. 2
of the
Charter
.
The
Court dismissed that claim and noted that marriage is a civil contract that
“may not be altered by private agreement of the parties or their religious
tenets” such that a party cannot demand exclusion of their marriage from the
provisions of the
Divorce Act
.

[
85
]

In
Gordon v Keyes

(1986),
1986 CanLII 6942 (NS SC)
,
72 NSR (2d) 172 (WL)
(NSSC) [
Gordon
]
,

the respondent husband
opposed the divorce on religious grounds. He argued that a divorce decree would
“violate a solemn undertaking” that was made “to be the petitioner’s husband,
‘for as long as we both shall live’”. While the divorce decree had already been
granted in that case, the Court commented on the tenacity of the husband’s
religious arguments. The Court held that not only was it too late to oppose the
already-granted divorce, but that “our law does not recognize any religious
grounds of opposition. Divorce is a secular creature of statue law, and
religion has played no part in the grant of divorce since before 1857 when
divorce jurisdiction was vested in the ecclesiastical courts of England” (at
para. 14).

[
86
]

Also, in
Acchione v
Acchione
,
1988 CarswellOnt 1431
(WL)

(Ont H Ct J)
, the Ontario Supreme Court
dealt with a similar scenario, whereby the husband opposed the divorce on
grounds of religious and moral principles. Since the criteria for divorce had
been established, the Court found that it was “obliged in law” to grant the
divorce, regardless of whether the husband agreed with it or not.

[
87
]

Numerous cases across
Canada have commented on the reasons for which severance may be granted. As
mentioned above, the decision is inherently discretionary. Different courts have
adopted different approaches to severance and have required different
thresholds to be met when determining whether severance is appropriate. For
example, as cited by counsel for Mr. Van Burgsteden, courts in Ontario have
held that requests for severance of divorce from corollary matters are “almost
routinely granted” and that the party opposing severance must show that
severance would cause a legal disadvantage. (
Al-Saati v Fahmi,
2015 ONSC
1114
,
59 RFL (7th) 219
[
Al-Saati
]
).

[
88
]

However, in Manitoba, a
slightly more stringent approach to severance has been adopted.
In
Winstanley
,

the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench noted that severance is not a matter of
right and even in situations where the applicant is able to establish criteria
to support an application for severance, the Court retains discretion to deny a
motion for severance. Additionally,
in
Desjardins v Desjardins
(1993),
1993 CanLII 15105 (MB QB)
,
89
Man R (2d) 140
,

the Court noted that in family law proceedings,
severance should not be granted easily as it is preferable to have all matters
resolved together. According to the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench
in
Spiring
v Spiring
,
2004 MBQB 258
,
[2005] 6 WWR 737
[
Spiring
]
,

the
reluctance to sever the divorce proceedings from other matters relates to what
is referred to as judicial tidiness, “whereby a court usually prefers spouses
to complete their domestic issues before granting a change in marital status”
(at para. 18).

[
89
]

Saskatchewan courts
appear to have adopted a middle ground between these two approaches. While they
have not held that severance should be granted sparingly, they have also not
opined that severance should be granted liberally. In
the decisions in
Yung
,

Behnami
, and
Theriault
discussed
above, this Court reiterated
that the decision of whether to grant severance of the divorce from corollary
matters is discretionary and should be judiciously determined on a case-by-case
basis taking into consideration the impact of delay in granting the relief and
whether any party will suffer prejudice or irreparable harm (
Behnami
at

para
15
). Although there is no closed list of considerations, the evidence
should identify a genuine and substantive reason for the granting of the
relief. I would add, the mere possibility of a reconciliation advanced by one
of the parties as a ground to adjourn the application is not sufficient. There
must be a realistic possibility of reconciliation on the evidence before the Court
such that the Court is required to adjourn the application in accordance with

s. 10
of the
Divorce Act
.

(b)       Has
Ms. Jewitt established that the granting of a severed judgment for divorce will
result in prejudice to her such that the Court should not grant the same?

[
90
]

The requisite criteria
for divorce, including residency, separation in excess of one year
,
the
absence of collusion and no possibility of reconciliation have been established
by Mr. Van Burgsteden in this matter. There are no children of the marriage for
whom reasonable support must be determined prior to the divorce. With the
prerequisite criteria for divorce established, the question is whether
severance is appropriate in these circumstances.

[
91
]

In Mr. Van Burgsteden’s
affidavit, he provides reasons as to why he is seeking severance of the divorce
judgment from the other matters. Specifically, Mr. Van Burgsteden indicates
there is no possibility of reconciliation between the parties. He wishes to
marry his new common law spouse but cannot do so until he obtains a divorce. He
notes delays in the proceedings between the parties and anticipates the
likelihood of additional delays due to the lack of cooperation exhibited by Ms.
Jewitt, including with respect to acknowledging service of process and complying
with financial disclosure requirements. He also provides some detail on what he
calls incidents of “strange and unwanted attention” that he and his common law
spouse have received over the past few months as an explanation as to why
severance is desired. Other than his own speculation that Ms. Jewitt is behind
these incidents, he does not provide any evidence that connects this strange
and unwanted attention to the ongoing divorce proceedings. He believes if a
judgment for divorce was pronounced it would allow the parties respectively to
move forward in their separated lives. The question is whether these reasons
are sufficient to sever the divorce from the other matters.

[
92
]

I first note that there
have been numerous delays in this action, most of which have been caused by Ms.
Jewitt. She ignored efforts to serve the documents through email, she has
sought various adjournments, and she herself admits that she wanted to postpone
the proceedings until after she completed her medical degree due to her mental
health concerns.

[
93
]

Mr. Van Burgsteden
desires to move forward with his life and remarry. The following dates and
events are germane to this argument:

1.

on March 29, 2015,
the parties separated when Mr. Van Burgsteden moved out of the family home and
the parties began living separate and apart;

2.

the petition and property
statement of Mr. Van Burgsteden were filed on February 8, 2017, almost two
years after separation;

3.

on July 4, 2018, an
application was made to have service validated on Ms. Jewitt or to have the
time extended to serve the petition after Mr. Van Burgsteden had attempted to
serve Ms. Jewitt by email and received no response;

4.

an answer and
counter-petitioner were filed by Ms. Jewitt on November 13, 2018; and

5.

on December 7, 2018,
the petitioner brought an application for an order compelling the respondent to
produce information requested in a notice to disclose. A consent order was
issued whereby Ms. Jewitt agreed to provide copies of the documents requested
in the notice to disclose, dated May 3, 2018. However, on March 1, 2019, Ms.
Jewitt filed an objection to the notice to disclose. This forced the petitioner
to make another application for an order compelling the respondent to produce
the documents.

[
94
]

The parties have been
separated for over four years and little headway has been made in relation to
the proceedings. Regardless of the view on the rigidity in which severance
applications should be assessed, courts across Canada appear willing to grant
severance in many different types of circumstances. One of the circumstances
established by the case law that may give rise to a genuine and substantive reason
for severance is the remarriage of one of the divorcing spouses, which fits
squarely into the case at hand.

[
95
]

In
Spiring
,
a
motion for severance of the opposed divorce was granted. The wife opposed the
severance motion, alleging that it would cause further delay and that she would
suffer serious prejudice if the divorce proceeded in advance of the other outstanding
issues. Similar to this case, the husband in
Spiring
was living in a
common law relationship with another woman whom he wished to marry. He argued
that there was no realistic end in sight for the resolution of the litigation
and he did not want to put his life on hold any longer. The Court made the
following comments which are relevant to the case at hand:

12

Despite numerous motions, appearances and
case conferences, the parties are nowhere near ready for trial or for a
contested marital property accounting. Examinations for discovery are
scheduled for December 2004 and March 2005.

13
Although the husband has been seriously pressing
the litigation since January 2004, there has been little progress. Numerous
commitments have been made, mainly by the wife, at case conferences and then
not acted upon. There are two reasons for the delay. First, the wife became ill
and her treatments have interfered with her ability to focus on the litigation.
Secondly, counsel for the wife has not acted with due dispatch regarding
matters within his control. I note that the case conference judge has attempted
to balance the wife's health problems with the husband's desire to move the
litigation forward in imposing deadlines, commitments and scheduling. Despite
that balancing act, there appears to be far more missed deadlines than actual
forward progress. Likely, there will not be much progress until the wife's
health improves. Even the discovery dates are tentative and subject to the
wife's treatment schedule.

[
96
]

Despite Manitoba’s
reluctance to sever divorce proceedings from corollary matters as described
above and also
referenced in the
Spiring

decision itself, the Court
ordered severance due to the husband’s wish to remarry and the ongoing delay.
In doing so, the Court rejected the wife’s arguments in relation to prejudice.

[
97
]

Additionally,
in
Hildebrandt
v Hildebrandt,
2009 MBQB 52
,
238 Man R (2d) 71
[
Hildebrandt
]
, the
Court found that failure to grant severance when one party seeks to remarry can
cause prejudice to the spouse who wishes to remarry (at para. 21).
In

Hildebrandt
, the parties had been separated for almost four years and Ms. Hildebrandt
wished to remarry. The husband opposed severance, arguing that it would
negatively impact his rights under
The

Homesteads Act
, CCSM, c
H80
.
The Court found that severance of the divorce should be granted
despite the husband’s opposition as there was no independent or compelling
reasons to otherwise refuse or delay the divorce.

[
98
]

In
Boyd v Boyd,
2008
ABQB 497
, a similar conclusion was reached. The husband applied to sever the
divorce proceedings from corollary matters as he wished to remarry his fiancée
immediately or as soon as possible due to immigration issues. The parties had
lived separate and apart since 1997 and no steps were taken to finalize the
divorce until the husband decided he needed an immediate divorce to remarry.
The Court granted the motion to sever the divorce from the corollary matters
but placed timelines on the parties to move the litigation of the outstanding
issues forward.

[
99
]

In
Jones-Hannem v
Hannem,
2012 BCSC 1649
, the British Columbia Supreme Court noted that while
splitting issues in a proceeding risks “litigating in slices”, the Court will
permit issues to be severed if doing so best serves the interests of justice.
The Court noted that one party wanting a divorce in order to remarry or take
some other step in life was a “commonly accepted” reason to grant a divorce and
adjourn corollary matters. The idea that “the end of the marriage relationship
may remove an emotional roadblock to progress and thus spur the parties to
resolve the remaining issues” was explained as another reason to grant a
divorce prior to determining other matters. A similar sentiment was expressed
by Sandomirsky J. in the passage quoted above from
Yung
.

[
100
]

However, the wish to
remarry does not conclusively determine that severance should be granted. While
the wish to remarry may establish a
prima facie
case for severance, the
determination turns to whether severance will prejudice one of the spouses. For
example, in
Al-Khouri v Al-Khouri,
2011 NSSC 122
,
302 NSR (2d) 45
[
Al-Khouri
]
,
Mr. Al-Khouri sought severance for multiple reasons, one of them being that he
wished to marry his common law partner. Ms. Al-Khouri opposed severance. The
Court declined to grant severance as Mr. Al-Khouri had not proven on a balance
of probabilities that severance was appropriate in the circumstances.
Additionally, Ms. Al-Khouri would suffer financial prejudice if severance was
granted as she likely had a maintenance claim against her husband and her
husband had no life insurance. In the event of Mr. Al-Khouri’s death, the wife
would not have any access to maintenance if divorce had been granted. There
were also outstanding jurisdictional issues with ongoing Syrian divorce
proceedings.

[
101
]

In
Pokorski v
Pokorski,
2009 ABQB 276
,
472 AR 206
, the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench
also declined to grant severance despite the husband’s wish to remarry a
Russian who was currently on a tourist visa to Canada. The Court concluded that
severance would cause prejudice to Ms. Pokorski because she was less
financially able to deal with the delay than her husband and the husband’s
remarriage would impose upon him an additional support obligation which would
have to be taken into account when quantifying his obligation to Ms. Pokorksi.
Additionally, Mr. Pokorski would not have any incentive to pursue matrimonial
property division, which his wife wanted, if he received a divorce.

[
102
]

In
Butt v Mansoor,
2018
ABQB 927
, the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench also denied a severance
application as it concluded that severance would cause the wife prejudice. Mr.
Butt sought severance of the divorce proceedings from corollary matters so that
he could remarry. The corollary issue that remained outstanding was property
division. The Court concluded that severance would cause Ms. Mansoor prejudice
as Mr. Butt would have no incentive to ever resolve outstanding property
matters. Ms. Mansoor had not been dragging the litigation out and litigation
had proceeded quickly. The fact that Mr. Butt wanted to remarry weighed in
favour of severance but was found to not outweigh the other considerations.

[
103
]

The question of whether
Ms. Jewitt will suffer prejudice similar to the parties in the above-noted
cases must be determined. Ms. Jewitt raises several arguments to oppose
severance. First, she claims that
The
Family Maintenance Act, 1997

does
not provide for maintenance to be applied against an estate. Therefore, if
divorce was granted and the petitioner remarried and died prior to settling
outstanding issues, she alleges that she would be unable to execute her
existing claim for spousal maintenance against the estate. She
relies on
Al-Khouri

in support of this argument.

[
104
]

This is similar to the
argument advanced
in
Spiring
.
The wife argued that if her husband, who
was 47, died before the litigation was completed, she would be prejudiced
because as a non-spouse, she would lose rights under various legislation. The
Court rejected this argument, holding that there was no evidence that the
husband was in poor health or engaged in risky behaviour that might cause an
early death. They found that the Court was “asked to treat the death as a
possibility, however remote or theoretical” (at para. 34).

[
105
]

The same can be said
here. There is no evidence that Mr. Van Burgsteden is in poor health or engages
in risky behaviour that might cause an early death. The argument advanced is
theoretical and remote. If this was considered a factor in each decision,
severance could rarely, if ever, be granted.

[
106
]

Further, Ms. Jewitt’s
argument is flawed. Regardless of whether divorce is granted summarily or in
the ordinary course, she would be unable to exercise a claim of spousal support
against Mr. Van Burgsteden’s estate absent a court order or agreement between
the parties otherwise. Ms. Jewitt is the party claiming spousal support. There
is nothing preventing her from pursuing that claim. For whatever reason, she
has chosen not to do so in a timely manner. Her concerns for prejudice ring
hollow when it lies with her to bring the claim forward to a judicial or other
determination. Nevertheless, the evidence establishes that Mr. Van Burgsteden
is willing and has been financially supporting Ms. Jewitt, even in the absence
of court-ordered spousal support payments.

[
107
]

The prejudice she
alleges to her ability to pursue a support claim against Mr. Van Burgsteden’s
estate which could result from his remarriage and subsequent death prior to the
parties attaining a resolution of the corollary issues, is mitigated in these
circumstances in that she may continue her claims for division of family
property against Mr. Van Burgsteden’s estate. Further, a new spouse’s claims
for property division under
The
Family Property Act
are secondary to a
prior spouse’s claims (s. 51). Thus, she may continue to prosecute that
claim against Mr. Van Burgsteden’s estate in the event of his untimely demise
prior to a judicial or other determination.

[
108
]

Finally,
s
he also argues that the Court should decline to grant severance of the
divorce because of risk of prejudice to her or because of the absence of urgent
and compelling reasons on behalf of the petitioner. While she may not view Mr.
Van Burgsteden’s desire to remarry as a compelling reason given that, in her
view, he has demonstrated a “lack of adherence to commitment with regard to
marriage”, that is not determinative of the issue. As mentioned above,
remarriage is a factor that courts have consistently considered in severance
applications.

[
109
]

Ms. Jewitt also argues
that the divorce will be devastating and “may prejudice her financially,
professionally and psychologically.” She claims this constitutes irreparable
harm. She also warns that marital breakdown is associated with increased risk
of depression and that depression is associated with suicide and as a result,
divorce will not serve the greater public good. However, this misapprehends the
analysis in the circumstances of the severance motion. Courts focus on whether
severance will result in
legal prejudice
; not prejudice in other areas
of life. For example,
in
Al-Saati
,
the Ontario Supreme Court noted that
the party must show legal disadvantage. Additionally,
in
Spiring
,
the
Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench held that the Court must look for real prejudice
in the litigation, directly caused by the severance of the other issues. Mr.
Van Burgsteden is entitled to a divorce and regardless of whether it is granted
severally or through the ordinary course, the divorce may cause the same
psychological impacts on Ms. Jewitt. It would be reasonable for the Court to
anticipate Ms. Jewitt should be able to mitigate against any psychological
impacts of being civilly divorced from Mr. Van Burgsteden by pursuing
appropriate counselling and/or psychiatric care.

[
110
]

In all the
circumstances I determine this to be an appropriate case to grant the
application for a severed divorce. A
ccordingly, t
he divorce judgment shall issue. All other
outstanding issues between the parties are adjourned
sine die
.

[
111
]

Mr. Van Burgsteden
claims costs. He has been entirely successful in this application and has been
put to additional expense in having to address the constitutional questions
raised by Ms. Jewitt. I order costs in favour of Mr. Van Burgsteden and against
Ms. Jewitt in the fixed amount of $3,000 payable in any event of the cause. The
Attorney General of Canada did not seek costs and so none are awarded to the
Attorney General of Canada.
